edits.defect: DEFECT 1 — unflagged interpolation: israf glossed as desire 'demanding public legitimacy'
edits.before: *Israf* is going beyond due bounds. The ayah is not portraying desire as morally self-justifying. It is portraying desire that overran its boundary and then demanded public legitimacy.
edits.after:
*Israf* is going beyond due bounds, and the commentators keep the word tightly tied to exactly that. Al-Jalalayn glosses *musrifun* as *mutajawizuna al-halala ila al-haram* — going past the lawful into the forbidden. Al-Muyassar reads it as going past the limits Allah set. Al-Tabari puts Lut's charge in the plainest terms: *innakum la-qawmun ta'tuna ma harrama Allahu 'alaykum wa ta'sunahu bi-fi'likum hadha* — you are a people who come to what Allah has forbidden you, and disobey Him by this deed of yours.

So the word marks a line crossed. It is not a verdict on wanting as such. It is a statement about where the wanting went.
edits.evidence: No fetched edition carries a legitimacy-seeking element; all three that gloss *musrifun* gloss it as a boundary crossed. al-Jalalayn 7:81: 'بَلْ أنْتُمْ قَوْم مُسْرِفُونَ﴾ مُتَجاوِزُونَ الحَلال إلى الحَرام'. al-Muyassar 7:81: 'بل أنتم قوم متجاوزون لحدود الله في الإسراف في المعاصي والشهوات'. al-Tabari 7:81: '﴿بل أنتم قوم مسرفون﴾، يقول: إنكم لقوم تأتون ما حرَّم الله عليكم، وتعصونه بفعلكم هذا... وذلك هو الإسراف، في هذا الموضع'. Ibn Kathir's 7:80-81 block gives no gloss of *musrifun* at all, so it is not named. The people's *jawab* in 7:82 is *akhrijuhum min qaryatikum* — expulsion, not a demand for legitimation.

edits.defect: DEFECT 2 — ungrounded present-tense sociological program (Theme 1 section title)
edits.before: ### Theme 1: Public Sin Eventually Demands Public Moral Inversion
edits.after: ### Theme 1: In Lut's Town, the Ones Who Kept Away Were Named as the Problem
edits.evidence: The old title announced a general social law about how societies behave; no edition supports a claim beyond this narrative. The new title states only what 7:82 reports — the town gave the abstention as its reason for the expulsion ('أَخْرِجُوهُم مِّن قَرْيَتِكُمْ ۖ إِنَّهُمْ أُنَاسٌ يَتَطَهَّرُونَ').

edits.defect: DEFECT 2 — ungrounded sociological program (Theme 1 body: 'wants language changed, shame displaced, standards mocked')
edits.before:
The people of Lut show that open corruption does not remain content with private permission. Over time it wants moral reversal. It wants language changed, shame displaced, standards mocked, and purity treated as aggression.

[PAUSE]

That is why their answer is exile. When a society grows attached to its corruption, righteous presence itself becomes unbearable. The problem is no longer simply what people are doing. The problem becomes what they must do to keep doing it without interruption from conscience.
edits.after:
Look closely at the sentence the townspeople actually produce. They give a reason for the expulsion, and the reason is not a crime. It is the keeping-away. Qatadah's comment on this line is preserved by both Ibn Kathir and al-Tabari: *'abuhum bi-ghayri 'ayb wa dhammuhum bi-ghayri dhamm* — they faulted them with what is no fault, and blamed them for what is no blame. The fault was manufactured. What the town wrote up as the offence was the one thing in the town that was not one.

[PAUSE]

Notice also who is being expelled. The command *akhrijuhum* is plural, though the passage up to that point had been speaking of Lut alone. Al-Tabari stops on that shift: what they meant was Lut and his household, or Lut and everyone in the town who held to his religion. Al-Jalalayn reads it the same way — Lut and his followers. The answer was not aimed only at the man who had spoken. It was aimed at everyone his speech had gathered.
edits.evidence: Only the 'purity treated as aggression' clause had any anchor, and only for the narrative: al-Tabari 7:82 report 14838, 'عن قتادة: ﴿إنهم أناس يتطهرون﴾، يقول: عابوهم بغير عَيْب، وذمُّوهم بغير ذَمّ', and Ibn Kathir 7:82, 'Qatadah commented, "They shamed them (Lut and the believers) with what is not a shame at all."' Two editions named individually, not a breadth claim. The plural-imperative observation is al-Tabari 7:82: 'إلا أن قال بعضهم لبعض: أخرجوا لوطًا وأهله= ولذلك قيل: "أخرجوهم"، فجمع، وقد جرى قبل ذكر "لوط" وحده دون غيره... أخرجوا لوطًا ومن كان على دينه من قريتكم', and al-Jalalayn 7:82: '﴿أخْرِجُوهُمْ﴾ أيْ لُوطًا وأَتْباعه'. 'Wants language changed' and 'standards mocked' had no basis in any edition and are gone.

edits.defect: DEFECT 2 — same defect in the Introduction: bolded general social law
edits.before: So the core warning here is not only about one condemned act. It is about what sustained rebellion does to public moral perception. **When transgression becomes communal culture, purity itself begins to look like provocation.**
edits.after: So the warning here is not only about one condemned act. It is also about the answer the town gave once the act was named. **In Lut's town, the keeping-away itself was entered as the reason for exile.**
edits.evidence: The bolded sentence was the file's single most quotable line and stated a universal claim about how societies behave, with no classical anchor. Narrowed to what 7:82 itself reports. Same pattern also narrowed in the Introduction's opening paragraph ('moves quickly to the social consequence of a people normalizing corruption: eventually the very presence of people who still care about purity feels intolerable' → 'moves quickly to what the town did when it was confronted: it moved to expel the people who kept away from what it was doing').

edits.defect: DEFECT 2 — closing line asserted as a law of moral decline
edits.before: That sentence should make us tremble. There is a point of moral decline at which people stop merely resisting truth and begin resenting those who still wish to live by it.
edits.after: That sentence should make us tremble, and it is worth being exact about why. The town did not simply act. It gave a reason, and the reason clause is *innahum unasun yatatahharun*. This reflection will not claim to know more than the ayah reports. It will only sit with the question the ayah leaves standing in the room: has anyone else's keeping-away ever felt, to me, like something aimed at me?
edits.evidence: Per the RUBRIC's REFLECTION-FLAGGED category: the line is now visibly the reflection's own contemplation ('This reflection will not claim to know more than the ayah reports'), and it is anchored to 7:82's own words — the reason clause إِنَّهُمْ أُنَاسٌ يَتَطَهَّرُونَ. No claim about how societies work remains.

edits.defect: DEFECT 3 — RUBRIC CHECK 4 failure: no tadabbur-vs-fatwa line, no scope statement
edits.before:
[PAUSE]

May Allah protect us from excess
edits.after:
[PAUSE]

One last thing, said plainly. This is a tadabbur — a reading of what the passage says, and of what the commentaries say about it. It is not a fatwa and it does not carry one. Questions of ruling belong to qualified scholars working in that discipline, where the classical authorities differed among themselves, and nothing here settles any of that. Nor is anything here addressed to judging a particular person. What the passage puts in front of the reader is a town, the answer it gave, its end, and then a command in the singular — *fa-unzur*, look — which is directed at the one doing the reading.

[PAUSE]

May Allah protect us from excess
edits.evidence: RUBRIC check 4 requires that an ahkam-adjacent passage distinguish tadabbur from fatwa. Ibn Kathir's own commentary on 7:83-84 closes with the Ibn 'Abbas hadith recorded by Ahmad, Abu Dawud, at-Tirmidhi and Ibn Majah, so a reader will meet the ruling question immediately outside this file; the scope line marks the boundary without importing it. Deliberately does NOT enumerate the fiqh positions and does NOT cite the punishment hadith. Follows the exemplar's closing move ('None of this is a legal ruling... For rulings, ask a qualified scholar'), in the file's own register. The *fa-unzur* framing is the ayah's own singular imperative (7:84) and al-Tabari's reading of it: 'فانظر، يا محمد، إلى عاقبة هؤلاء'.

edits.defect: DEFECT 4 — semantic overreach on yatatahharun ('daily practice' of cleanliness)
edits.before: This is one of the sharpest lines in the story. The verb *yatatahharun* is Form V of ط-ه-ر — *tafa''ala*, the reflexive-effortful pattern. It does not say "they are pure" (that would be a passive or a simple active participle). It says they are **working at purity**, actively making themselves pure. The form itself carries the image of sustained effort — someone bending their life toward cleanliness as a daily practice. That is what the society of Lut finds intolerable. Not pure people. *People who are trying.* What should have been praise becomes accusation. In a diseased moral environment, visible effort at purity begins to feel like judgment on those who have stopped trying. So rather than repent, the society tries to eliminate the contrast.
edits.after:
This is one of the sharpest lines in the story. The verb *yatatahharun* is Form V of ط-ه-ر — *tafa''ala*, the reflexive pattern. It does not say "they are pure" (that would be a passive or a simple active participle). It says they are **keeping themselves pure** — something held to, not something merely possessed.

And the commentators are specific about what is being kept away from. Al-Tabari glosses the phrase this way: Lut and those who followed him are people who keep clear of what we ourselves do. He then brings the same reading from Mujahid, and from Ibn 'Abbas, and from as-Suddi, who renders the verb *yataharrajun* — they hold back from it as from something forbidden. Al-Muyassar and al-Jalalayn read it just as narrowly: keeping clear of that one act.

So the word is not a picture of general daily cleanliness. It is abstention from the specific thing the town was doing. And that is what the town named as its reason for the expulsion. What should have been praise was entered as the charge.
edits.evidence: Morphology is unchanged and verified (corpus 7:82:20 = VF:5, root طهر; verify_morphology passes 35/35). Every fetched gloss reads the verb as abstention from the specific act: al-Tabari 7:82, '﴿إنهم أناس يتطهرون﴾، يقول: إن لوطًا ومن تبعه أناس يتنزهون عما نفعله نحنُ من إتيان الرجال في الأدبار'; Mujahid (reports 14834-14836) 'من أدبار الرجال وأدبار النساء'; Ibn 'Abbas (report 14836) likewise; as-Suddi (report 14837) 'يتحرَّجون'; al-Muyassar 7:82, 'أناس يتنزهون عن إتيان أدبار الرجال'; al-Jalalayn 7:82, '﴿إنّهُمْ أُناس يَتَطَهَّرُونَ﴾ مِن أدْبار الرِّجال'. Ibn Kathir carries Mujahid's narrow gloss too. Each edition named individually — no breadth claim. The trailing generalization ('In a diseased moral environment, visible effort at purity begins to feel like judgment on those who have stopped trying') was the same DEFECT 2 pattern and was narrowed to the narrative in the same contiguous block.
